subject: physics
title: Energy stores and systems
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Energy stores and systems — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.1.1.1.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Energy stores and systems, specification section 4.1.1.1.
final_note: You worked through Energy stores and systems — 13 specification statements.

concepts.def: A system is an object or group of objects. It is whatever you decide to treat as the thing you are studying — a single ball, or a ball and the Earth, or a kettle together with the water in it. Choosing the system first is what makes it possible to say clearly which stores are emptying and which are filling.

Energy in a system is described as being held in stores. When a system changes, there are changes in the way energy is stored: the amount of energy in some stores goes down and the amount in others goes up.

concepts.term: The energy stores used in this specification
concepts.def: The stores named across the AQA specification are: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. Heating, work done by forces, work done when a current flows and radiation are not stores — they are the ways energy gets from one store to another.

concepts.term: Describing all the changes in a system
concepts.def: A full description names the store or stores that empty, the store or stores that fill, and the way the energy was transferred between them. 'All the changes' includes the small ones — the thermal stores of the surroundings that fill because of friction or air resistance are part of the answer, not an optional extra.

As the object rises, its kinetic store empties and its gravitational potential store fills; air resistance also fills the thermal store of the object and the surroundings. At the highest point the object is momentarily at rest, so its kinetic store is empty and its gravitational potential store is at its largest. On the way down the changes run the other way.

concepts.term: A moving object hitting an obstacle
concepts.def: The kinetic store of the moving object empties. Energy fills the thermal stores of the object, of the obstacle and of the surroundings, and some is carried away by sound waves. If either object is squashed and springs back, an elastic potential store fills and then empties again.

concepts.term: An object accelerated by a constant force
concepts.def: The force does work on the object as the object moves. Work done by the force fills the kinetic store of the object, so the object speeds up. Because work done = force × distance, acting over a longer distance transfers more energy to the kinetic store, even though the force is unchanged.

The kinetic store of the vehicle empties. Friction forces in the brakes do work, filling the thermal store of the brakes; friction at the tyres and air resistance fill thermal stores too. The hot brakes then transfer energy to the thermal store of the surroundings as they cool.

concepts.term: Bringing water to a boil in an electric kettle
concepts.def: A current flows in the heating element, so work is done and the thermal store of the element fills. The element heats the water, filling the thermal store of the water. The thermal stores of the kettle body and of the surrounding room also fill, and once the water boils, energy is carried away by the escaping steam.

concepts.term: The three ways a system is changed
concepts.def: Throughout the Energy section, the energy change when a system is changed is calculated for three routes: heating, work done by forces, and work done when a current flows. Each is a way of transferring energy into or out of stores, and each is measured in joules.

concepts.term: Calculating an energy change by heating
concepts.def: ΔE = m c Δθ, that is change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, with ΔE in joules (J), m in kilograms (kg), c in J/kg °C and Δθ in °C. This equation is supplied on the Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled — but Δθ is the change in temperature, not the final temperature.

concepts.term: Calculating work done by a force
concepts.def: W = F s, that is work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force), with W in joules (J), F in newtons (N) and s in metres (m). This equation must be recalled. If the object does not move along the line of action of the force, no work is done by that force, however large the force is.

concepts.term: Calculating work done when a current flows
concepts.def: P = E/t, that is power = energy transferred / time, with P in watts (W), E in joules (J) and t in seconds (s). This equation must be recalled, and it rearranges to E = P t. Time must be in seconds: a three-minute boil is 180 s, not 3.

Every energy change — by heating, by work done by forces, or by work done when a current flows — is measured in the same unit, the joule (J). That shared unit is what makes it possible to put all the changes in one system side by side and compare them directly.

concepts.term: Showing redistribution on a common scale
concepts.def: Once each change has been calculated in joules, the amounts can be drawn as bars on one shared scale, showing how the energy in the system was redistributed. The energy is not lost or created: the amounts shown after the change add up to the amount shown before it, spread differently among the stores.

mcqs.q: In physics, what is meant by a system?
options: A machine that transfers energy.
An object or a group of objects.
A group of objects, never just one.
A place where energy is kept.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition, word for word.

mcqs.q: The specification says there are changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes. Which statement describes this correctly?
options: Some stores empty while other stores fill up.
Energy is gradually used up as the system changes.
Energy is changed into a different type of energy.
New energy is created somewhere in the system.
mcqs.explain: This is exactly what a change in the way energy is stored means.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an energy store?
options: Heating a beaker of water with a flame.
A current flowing through a heater wire.
The kinetic store of a moving trolley.
Sound waves spreading out from a bell.
mcqs.explain: Kinetic is one of the stores named in the specification, and the trolley holds energy in it.

mcqs.q: A ball rolls down a slope. Which description best meets the requirement to describe all the changes in the way energy is stored?
options: Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy.
Energy is transferred from the top of the slope to the bottom.
The ball uses up its energy as it rolls down to the bottom.
The gravitational store empties; the kinetic and thermal stores fill.
mcqs.explain: It names the store that empties, the stores that fill, and includes the thermal store filled by friction.

mcqs.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored as it rises?
options: The kinetic store empties and the gravitational potential store fills.
The gravitational potential store empties and the kinetic store fills up.
The kinetic store and the gravitational potential store both keep filling.
The kinetic store empties and the elastic potential store fills instead.
mcqs.explain: The ball slows as it gains height, so the kinetic store empties as the gravitational potential store fills.

mcqs.q: At the highest point of its flight, a ball thrown straight upwards is momentarily at rest. What is true of its energy stores at that moment?
options: Its gravitational store is at its largest and its kinetic store is empty.
Its kinetic store still holds energy, or it could not fall back down.
Its gravitational store is empty because it has stopped moving up.
Both its kinetic and gravitational stores are empty at that instant.
mcqs.explain: It is at its greatest height and is not moving, so the gravitational store is full and the kinetic store empty.

mcqs.q: A moving trolley crashes into a wall and stops. Which describes the main change in the way energy is stored?
options: The kinetic store empties into thermal stores of both objects.
The kinetic store of the trolley is destroyed by the wall impact.
The kinetic store passes into the kinetic store of the wall itself.
The kinetic store of the trolley becomes a store of sound waves.
mcqs.explain: The trolley and the wall both warm slightly, and the surroundings do too; this is where the energy goes.

mcqs.q: A cyclist rides into a hedge and stops. A student says all the energy has gone into the hedge. Why is this description incomplete?
options: A hedge cannot store energy because a hedge does not move.
Thermal stores of the cyclist, bike and surroundings also fill.
The cyclist's kinetic store is used up, not transferred at all.
The kinetic store of the hedge fills as the cyclist stops.
mcqs.explain: Energy fills thermal stores on both sides of the collision, plus the surroundings, and sound carries some away.

mcqs.q: A constant horizontal force pushes a box along a very smooth floor. Which describes the change in the way energy is stored?
options: The kinetic store of the box stays the same as it keeps moving.
The gravitational store of the box fills as it is pushed.
Work done by the force fills the kinetic store of the box.
The energy from the push is used up as the box moves.
mcqs.explain: The force acts along the direction of movement, so it does work and the box accelerates.

mcqs.q: The same constant force accelerates a trolley over twice the distance. How does this change the energy transferred to the kinetic store?
options: It stays the same, because the force has not changed.
It doubles, because work done is force times distance.
It halves, because the force is spread over more distance.
It doubles, but only if the trolley is twice as heavy.
mcqs.explain: W = F s, so doubling s with F unchanged doubles the energy transferred.

mcqs.q: A driver brakes and the car slows down. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored?
options: The kinetic store empties and thermal stores of the brakes fill.
The kinetic store empties and is used up by the brakes.
The kinetic store is destroyed by the friction in the brakes.
The kinetic store empties into the gravitational store of the car.
mcqs.explain: Friction forces in the brakes do work, filling their thermal store; the tyres and air do so too.

mcqs.q: A few minutes after a car has braked and stopped, its brakes have cooled back down. What has happened to the energy?
options: It has been transferred to thermal stores in the surroundings.
It has been destroyed as the brakes cooled down again afterwards.
It has gone back into the kinetic store of the car that stopped.
It stays in the thermal store of the brakes for ever afterwards.
mcqs.explain: Anything hotter than its surroundings transfers energy to them until the temperatures match.

mcqs.q: Water is brought to the boil in an electric kettle. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored?
options: The electrical store of the kettle empties into the water.
The chemical store of the water fills up as it gets hotter.
Heat energy is made in the element and stored in the water.
Work is done as a current flows; the water's thermal store fills.
mcqs.explain: A current in the element does work, filling the thermal store of the element and then of the water.

mcqs.q: A kettle boils a full jug of water. Which statement about where the energy ends up is correct?
options: All of it goes into the thermal store of the water inside the kettle.
Most goes to the water's thermal store, some to the kettle and room.
All of it is used up in making the water change into steam.
Most goes to the room and only a little goes into the water.
mcqs.explain: The kettle body is warm afterwards and steam escapes, so those stores fill as well as the water's.

mcqs.q: A kettle heats 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Using ΔE = m c Δθ, which is given on the Physics equation sheet, how much energy is transferred to the thermal store of the water?
mcqs.explain: ΔE = 0.50 × 4200 × 80 = 168 000 J, using the temperature change of 80 °C.

mcqs.q: 0.40 kg of cooking oil is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. The specific heat capacity of the oil is 2000 J/kg °C. How much energy is transferred to the thermal store of the oil?
A constant force of 20 N moves a box of mass 4.0 kg a distance of 3.0 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done by the force?
mcqs.explain: W = F s = 20 × 3.0 = 60 J. The mass is not needed.

mcqs.q: A student holds a heavy box completely still, at arm's length, for 30 s. How much work is done by the student on the box?
options: A large amount, because a big force is needed to hold the box up.
None, because the box does not move in the direction of the force.
It depends on the time, because holding it for longer is harder.
It equals the weight of the box multiplied by the arm's length.
mcqs.explain: W = F s, and s is zero, so the work done on the box is zero however large the force.

mcqs.q: An electric heater has a power of 2000 W and is switched on for 3.0 minutes. Using P = E/t, how much energy is transferred by the heater?
mcqs.explain: E = P t = 2000 × 180 = 360 000 J, with the time converted to seconds.

mcqs.q: A current flows through the heating element of a kettle. Which statement describes what is happening?
options: Electrical energy is stored in the element as current flows.
The current is used up as it passes through the hot element.
Work is done, and the thermal store of the element fills.
The element creates energy from the current flowing inside it.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's route: work done when a current flows fills a thermal store.

mcqs.q: While boiling water, a kettle element transfers 180 000 J. Of this, 168 000 J fills the thermal store of the water and 9 000 J fills the thermal store of the kettle body. On a common scale, how much is shown transferred to the surroundings?
mcqs.explain: 180 000 − 168 000 − 9 000 = 3 000 J, so the amounts after add up to the amount before.

mcqs.q: A bar chart on a common scale shows the energy in each store of a system before and after it changes. What should be true of the bars?
options: The bars after add up to less, because energy is used up.
Every bar after the change is smaller than it was before.
The bars are drawn on separate scales so all can be seen.
The bars after add up to the same total as the bars before.
mcqs.explain: The energy is redistributed among the stores, so the totals match; that is what the common scale shows.
